deliverables.title: Executive Summary
deliverables.summary: The leadership-facing distillation of Phase 0: DAS holds rich customer data across dozens of systems but has no way to recognize one person across them ("we don't" was the answer when asked how identity resolves today), and the legacy join key meant to do it was found all-zero and non-functional. It states the finding, recommends a productionized open-source CDP as DAS's system of record, and shows that closing Phase 0 converts an assessment into a buildable, fixed-scope program backed by a working golden record from real data.
deliverables.detail:
DAS has abundant customer data and no single view of a customer: the same consumer is a separate, disconnected record in the CRM, DMS, email, and ad platforms, with nothing tying them together. Phase 0 set out to answer one question — is a golden record achievable from DAS's real data? — and answers it with a demonstrated record, a locked identity strategy, a privacy framework, a costed build plan, and a cloud-agnostic architecture.

### What we found
- No identity resolution exists today; asked how it's done, DAS said *"we don't"* — the recommended fix is the golden record, with a working view live at `/analysis/artifacts/golden-record/`.
- The legacy join key (CommonClientID) was audited and found all-zero / non-functional (audit 2026-06-14, `memory/decisions.md`), so the CDP must build identity from first principles.
- The plumbing is fragile: 13 SSIS jobs near capacity and confirmed for retirement, reporting on Juicebox (221 reports) DAS won't keep, and the estate split across AWS (source data) and Azure (apps/event bus) — no single home for a customer system.

### What we recommend
- A productionized CDP on a portable open-source core as DAS's system of record, so the legacy SSIS/EDW stack can be retired once it's reliable (`docs/cdp-architecture.md`).
- Identity: deterministic-first (exact match on email/phone/VIN/dealer ID + human review queue), ML earned later once Phase 1 review decisions become training data — locked as "Option A, 2026-06-17" (`docs/deliverables/identity-resolution-strategy.md`).
- Deletion-first, tenant-isolated privacy by construction; reporting on self-hosted Apache Superset at $0 license baseline replacing Juicebox; cloud is DAS's choice — a first-party cost comparison (2026-06-22) shows the clouds within ~3% (~$130/mo), Azure-primary preferred (`docs/cloud-aws-vs-azure-bakeoff.md`).

### Scope and path forward
- Phase 1 (Build): 1a platform foundation (~4 months, derived from sized backlog ÷ team capacity, not asserted) + 1b migration; Phase 2 applications (VSS retool, service, marketing, mobile) on the golden record; Phase 3 AI/ML on Phase-1-labeled data (`docs/deliverables/detailed-phase-1-2-plans.md`).
- Run-cost modeled as a planning guide, not a quote: ~$1,140/mo dev baseline during 1a phasing toward ~$4,460/mo at production (±30–40% until production load observed).
- Closing Phase 0 converts the assessment into a buildable, fixed-scope program that drops into a prioritized backlog and SOW (`docs/deliverables/cdp-scoping-document.md`).
- Full deliverable: `docs/deliverables/executive-summary.md`

### Four views (each an annotated summary — dig in)
- **Target-State Data Flow** — sources to bronze to resolve to golden record to serving.
- **Services Topology** — the services and the boundaries between them.
- **Deployment Architecture** — Kubernetes, managed tier, observability, DR.

components.title: Target-State Data Flow
components.summary: The target-state data flow is the end-to-end view of how a consumer or vehicle record travels through the CDP — from the moment it leaves an original source to the moment a downstream app reads it. It matters to DAS because it replaces the fragile nightly SSIS rebuild with a continuous, traceable pipeline where the CDP itself becomes the system of record, ingesting from true origins rather than the summarized reporting views the team has said it does not trust.
components.detail:
This view expands one of the four layers of the consolidated architecture: how data actually moves. Today, data reaches users through a chain DAS is retiring — nightly SSIS jobs truncate and rebuild the warehouse, and pre-joined `DWRPT` views feed reporting, so consumer data is only ever as current as last night's run and only as trustworthy as views that may have been summarized along the way (SSIS deep-dive with Rick Sorich, 2026-06-08; `docs/cdp-architecture.md`). The target state inverts this: the CDP becomes the system of record and ingests from the original sources, never from EDW/DWRPT.

### One pipeline, four ways in
- Every record — whatever the channel — runs the same path: land raw, normalize, validate, resolve identity, store canonical, serve (`docs/cdp-architecture.md` Layer 1; `specs/03-phase-1-build/04-ingest/00-feature.md`).
- The four front doors are webhook, event stream, bulk upload, and batch pull; a new source is a single declarative registry entry, not a new system (`specs/03-phase-1-build/04-ingest/06-source-registry.md`).
- Event intake was set co-primary with batch, so a source can graduate from batch to real-time by flipping one field with no redesign (Dan Aston, decided 2026-06-12).

### Why DAS asked for it this way
- Raw lands untouched in an encrypted bronze store first, making the whole pipeline replayable — capture at the point of consumption was DAS's explicit, unprompted requirement (decided 2026-06-18, Leo; client-confirmed 2026-06-12).
- Intake is bus-agnostic on a NATS backbone; DAS's Azure Event Grid connects via a config-only adapter with no compute we run on their side (`specs/03-phase-1-build/04-ingest/08-event-grid-webhook-adapter.md`).
- Change-data-capture (Debezium) streams source inserts, updates, and deletes continuously, so the CDP reflects changes as they happen, not at the next batch window (`specs/03-phase-1-build/04-ingest/12-cdc-capture-debezium.md`).

### What is locked, what firms up at build
- Locked with dates and owners: the four-channel/one-pipeline shape, bus-agnostic raw-first intake, deterministic-first identity (Option A, 2026-06-17), and the bitemporal append-only storage and provenance model (2026-06-18, Alicia + Luis).
- Build-time only: the Event Grid subscription wiring, CDC connector tuning against live source DBs, and the per-source registry entries — the architecture stands regardless of how these settle.
- Decision log behind every dated claim: `memory/decisions.md`.
- Full write-up: `docs/deliverables/target-state-data-flow.md`.

components.title: Services Topology
components.summary: The Services Topology defines the seven services that make up the CDP — what each one owns and the contracts that hold between them — described by job rather than by any cloud vendor's product name. It matters to DAS because clean service edges are what let the team build the four Phase 1 tracks in parallel, swap any single piece without disturbing the rest, and reason precisely about where customer data and trust flow across ~1,700 dealer tenants.
components.detail:
A CDP is not one program but a small set of services, each with a single job and a clear edge, governed by one principle: **one responsibility per service, one contract per boundary** (`docs/deliverables/services-topology.md`). The seven services group into ingestion, event intake, identity resolution, the Profile API, admin/ops, workflow/workers, and analytics/search — a decomposition that maps directly onto the foundation-plus-four-tracks structure of the build (`specs/03-phase-1-build/00-epic.md`). The backbone is a **portable OSS core that runs unchanged on either cloud**, so the AWS-vs-Azure bake-off settles the substrate without touching any boundary below (direction set 2026-06-17, `docs/cdp-architecture.md`).

### The two boundaries that do the work
- **Airflow owns all ingestion; Temporal owns the application** — no overlap, enforced by a CI guard so a slow backfill never competes with a live merge and each plane scales independently (decided 2026-06-13, `memory/decisions.md`).
- **Intake is bus-agnostic, the resolver is privileged, everything served is tenant-scoped** — events arrive through adapters not a hard-wired bus; the identity resolver runs above tenant row-level security because cross-dealer matching is its whole point, while every other read and write stays inside one dealer's boundary (matching model locked 2026-06-18, Alicia + Luis).

### What is locked
- **Four-channel, raw-first, replayable ingestion** with a config-driven source registry where sources are data, not code — a source graduates from batch to event by flipping one field (raw-landing rationale, Leo 2026-06-18).
- **NATS JetStream as the internal backbone, RabbitMQ for app messaging**, with DAS's Azure Event Grid bridging in as a config-only CloudEvents 1.0 adapter (co-primary event path, Dan Aston 2026-06-12; NATS/RabbitMQ split settled 2026-06-17).
- **Dual-surface Profile API** (Django REST + Strawberry GraphQL) on a Python-primary backend, with Apache Superset as the self-hosted reporting layer for ~1,700 dealer tenants (language strategy and Superset both 2026-06-14; VSS is the first downstream consumer).

### What firms up at build time
- The source-registry entries themselves (added through the long tail), the Event Grid subscription details, and the cloud substrate — none of which change the boundaries above (`docs/cdp-architecture.md`, honest constraints).
- **Full write-up, the service diagram, and the four contracts:** `docs/deliverables/services-topology.md`.

components.title: Deployment Architecture
components.summary: The Deployment Architecture view explains how the CDP is actually run, shipped, and recovered: a portable open-source core on Kubernetes alongside a thin layer of managed cloud services, sized to start small and rightsize on real load. It matters to DAS because it proves the platform is cloud-neutral by construction (Azure-primary preferred, AWS a live alternative), reproducible as code, and recoverable without a rebuild — so the cloud choice is a documented business decision, not an architectural lock-in.
components.detail:
This view answers a single decision-maker question: once the CDP is built, how does it run, ship, and recover — and does the choice of cloud change any of that? The shape is a deliberate split: DAS self-hosts the open-source software that defines the product (so it is identical on either cloud, with no managed-service premium and no vendor lock-in in app code) and leases the undifferentiated infrastructure — database of record, cache, object storage, ingress, secrets — where a cloud provider's HA, backups, and patching are worth paying for. Every shape traces to a dated decision and a canonical source; the full write-up is the deliverable doc below.

### What runs where, and how we know it works
- The OSS core (Django/Next.js, NATS JetStream, RabbitMQ, Temporal, Airflow, OpenSearch, Debezium) runs as pods on a Kubernetes node group; PostgreSQL, Redis, object storage, ingress, and secrets are managed services — the self-host-vs-managed split set in `docs/cdp-architecture.md` (Deployment) and detailed in `docs/cdp-reference-topology.md`.
- Observability is portable by design: OpenTelemetry feeds metrics to Prometheus/Grafana, logs to OpenSearch, and distributed traces to Jaeger — all OSS the team operates, identical on either cloud, with managed backends (AMP/Azure Monitor, X-Ray) as opt-in levers, not defaults (`docs/cdp-architecture.md`, Observability).

### Posture: start small, rightsize on real load
- We ship a dev baseline first and rightsize production against observed telemetry rather than guessing capacity up front — the infra-sizing decision of 2026-06-16 (`memory/decisions.md`, d-007). Moving dev → prod is a configuration change (more replicas, bigger nodes, an extra Postgres read replica), not a redesign.
- How it is built and recovered: all infrastructure is Terraform via `boilerworks-opscode` (no click-ops); production promotion is a push-button release gated by human approval with zero-downtime migrations; DR is a cross-region pilot-light Postgres standby plus geo-replicated, replayable object storage — bounding recovery to a promotion, not a rebuild.

### Where the cloud is decided
- The deployment is cloud-neutral: each managed swap-point has a documented Azure and AWS equivalent. Azure-primary is preferred to consolidate on DAS's org cloud (Dan Aston, 2026-06-17, `memory/decisions.md` d-091/d-093); AWS stays a live alternative on source-database data gravity (originally 2026-06-13, d-062).
- The cost re-verification on 2026-06-22 found the two clouds within ~3% at the Postgres-native baseline — effectively cost-neutral — so the choice is a DAS business call, not an architectural one (`docs/cloud-aws-vs-azure-bakeoff.md`).
- Full write-up: `docs/deliverables/deployment-architecture.md`.

components.title: Alignment with DAS's Cloud Footprint
components.summary: How the CDP's target architecture fits the cloud environment DAS already runs — a split estate where the source data lives on AWS but DAS standardizes its applications and event layer on Azure. It matters because it shows the CDP can land on either cloud without a redesign, prices both paths honestly, and leaves the final cost/benefit call with DAS rather than presuming it.
components.detail:
DAS does not run on one cloud, and the CDP is built to respect that. Its source databases (SQL Server on EC2, MySQL on RDS) sit on AWS — that is the data gravity — while DAS names Azure as its org-primary cloud and publishes its application events through Azure Event Grid (confirmed by Dan Aston 2026-06-17, `memory/decisions.md` d-090). The architecture is therefore cloud-neutral by design: a portable open-source core that runs unchanged on either substrate, with only a small set of managed-service swap-points differing between them. This view annotates how that alignment was reached and what it costs.

### The split estate and what we reuse
- Source data is anchored on AWS; the application and event layer is on Azure — so ingestion crosses a cloud boundary somewhere no matter where the CDP lands (`docs/cdp-architecture.md`, Cloud footprint alignment).
- The CDP reuses what DAS already has — Auth0 (cloud-neutral, federates EntraID) and the existing source databases (read-only, never replaced); legacy `3BHS001` is touched cautiously via read replica because its dependencies aren't fully mapped.
- Everything else (Kubernetes, NATS, Temporal, PostgreSQL, OpenSearch, Airflow) is net-new and portable; the app code never names a cloud (no vendor lock-in), decided as the portable-OSS-core direction 2026-06-17 (`memory/decisions.md` d-091).

### The cost read and the recommendation
- The backbone is cost-neutral at the Postgres-native baseline — roughly $4,451/mo AWS vs $4,583/mo Azure (~3%), per the bake-off verified 2026-06-22; unit prices are firm, monthly totals are ±30–40% planning figures (no production load observed yet).
- A prior "AWS cheaper at scale" claim rested on a phantom per-vCPU AKS surcharge; that meter does not exist (corrected against the live Azure Retail Prices API 2026-06-22), which is what leaves the backbone neutral.
- Direction set 2026-06-17 (Dan Aston): **Azure-primary preferred**, with AWS the credible data-gravity alternative; cost is not a blocker and **no cloud decision is recorded** — DAS makes the final call (`docs/cdp-architecture.md`, Locked decisions).

### Go deeper
- Full side-by-side pricing, component mapping, gaps, and verified rate catalog: `docs/cloud-aws-vs-azure-bakeoff.md`.
- The complete write-up this card annotates: `docs/deliverables/cloud-alignment.md`.

deliverables.title: DAS CDP Roadmap
deliverables.summary: The phased build plan that sequences DAS's CDP from a tested platform slice through full source migration, operator applications, and earned AI/ML — with relative T-shirt sizing and an AWS-vs-Azure run-cost model that together back a fixed-scope SOW. It matters because it lets DAS see what lands when, what each phase gates on, and what the platform costs to run before committing budget, while keeping scope synced to a single backlog source of truth.
deliverables.detail:
The roadmap stages the build so value lands early and downstream phases overlap rather than wait. Scope and sizing are derived from the project backlog (`specs/manifest.json`), the single source of truth; the phase model and cost model are planning overlays that group and cost the work without moving stories between phases. Effort is relative T-shirt sizing (S→EPIC), deferring committed schedule and labor cost to the SOW.

### Phase model — what lands when
- **1a Platform** (~4 months, derived from live sizing ÷ modeled AI-assisted team capacity, not asserted): platform substrate plus one tested source per channel across the 5 intake primitives (DB/API/SFTP/event/feed), backend + data model, read surfaces + search, identity resolution + curation, segmentation, and a Superset/RLS reporting baseline — see `docs/deliverables/identity-resolution-strategy.md` for the deterministic-first engine (Option A, 2026-06-17).
- **1b Long-tail migration**: the 16 remaining source onboards, SSIS reimplementation (EPIC), Juicebox/DWRPT→Superset report migration (EPIC), legacy deprecation — sequenced last and heaviest.
- **2 Enhancements + Applicatives**: activation/delivery, reporting parity, syndication, and apps on the CDP (VSS retool flagship, maintenance, marketing, mobile) — deliberately starts before 1b finishes at "critical data mass" so apps aren't blocked on the full long tail.
- **3a External AI then 3b own ML**: integrate hosted AI (`ai.das-technology.com`) first; build DAS's own pairwise/GNN identity ML later, trained on Phase-1 curation decisions (earned, not assumed; AI/ML schema ships empty-but-complete in Phase 1, so no migration).

### Sizing basis & run-cost
- Each story carries a T-shirt size mapping to both story-points and an engineering-day band; the mapping is canonical in `specs/estimate-bands.json` and totals are computed live (`specs/estimates.html`), never hand-entered — Phase 1 build ≈ 913 points / 456.5–894 engineering-days.
- Infrastructure run-cost (rightsize-on-load topology, 2026-06-16): dev ~$1,140/mo, prod ~$4,460/mo, near cloud-neutral (~3% apart) at Postgres-native; managed warehouse ~even between clouds since AWS's 4-RPU Redshift floor (Synapse pay-per-scan the Azure lever). Unit rates first-party-verified 2026-06-22; quantities are estimates, so totals are ±30–40% planning figures, not a quote. Azure-primary preferred (DAS org cloud), AWS the alternative — no cloud decision recorded yet (`docs/cloud-aws-vs-azure-bakeoff.md`, `docs/cdp-reference-topology.md`).
- Full deliverable: `docs/deliverables/detailed-phase-1-2-plans.md`.

roadmap.detail: Discovery (data source audit, identity landscape, infrastructure inventory) plus the architecture and platform-decision design. Output: this set of deliverables.

Builds the productionized CDP backend (V1) on the portable OSS core, in two sub-phases. 1a — Platform: the full platform ready and tested with one source ingest per channel (the 5 intake primitives — DB / API / SFTP / event / feed) — Foundation, Backend & Data Model, Frontend + read surfaces + search, Identity Resolution + Curation, Segmentation, the Ingest framework, and the Superset reporting baseline. ~4 months (gut-check). MVP is a thin slice inside 1a. 1b — Long-tail migration: onboard all remaining sources, reimplement SSIS, migrate reporting (Juicebox/DWRPT → Superset/warehouse), deprecate legacy. Cloud target is a client choice (Azure-primary preferred, AWS alternative, per the bake-off); the OSS core deploys on either. Infra run-cost: dev baseline ~$1.1k/mo during 1a, prod ~$4.5k/mo phasing in toward 1b (see Detailed Phase 1 & 2 Plans). Workstreams below derive from specs/manifest.json.

roadmap.focus: Applications · Enhancements + Applicatives (can start before 1b at critical data mass)
roadmap.detail: Applications and outbound delivery on the Phase-1 CDP — deliberately able to start before 1b completes, once enough sources are live to be valuable. All infrastructure ships in Phase 1 (segmentation + targeting and the web-UI, the reporting platform, consent + vault erasure, web-UI admin). Two sub-phases. Enhancements: outbound activation & delivery (Meta/TikTok/email/CRM connectors over the Phase-1 NATS backbone, website pixel / JS SDK, event-stream activation); reporting parity (custom-report catalog + self-serve, store-neutral); data exposure & syndication. Applicatives: applications on the CDP — VSS retool (flagship), maintenance/service (CarPlay/mobile), marketing activation, mobile, and data-enrichment — each consuming the golden record / events / consent instead of re-solving identity.

roadmap.focus: AI / ML · 3a External AI → 3b Own ML
roadmap.detail: Advanced intelligence on the unified data, in two sub-phases. 3a — External AI integration: integrate hosted/external AI against the CDP's governed access API (reuse DAS's ai.das-technology.com layer), LLM-assisted conflict review, agentic surfaces. 3b — Build-our-own ML: Tier 2 pairwise classifier and Tier 3 embeddings + GNN matching for identity, trained on the labeled merge/curation decisions Phase 1 produces. Architected for in Phase 1 — the AI/ML tables and resolver extension points ship empty-but-complete, so both add with zero schema migration.

components.title: CDP Scoping Document
components.summary: The core Phase 0 scoping report: it maps the ~85 customer-data sources DAS must onboard, defines the unified golden-record data model the CDP builds from them, specifies the config-driven ingest architecture replacing the failing SSIS stack, and registers six material risks each with a held posture. It is the document that converts DAS's scattered, near-capacity legacy data estate into a prioritized, buildable backlog with every claim traced to a dated decision.
components.detail:
DAS's customer knowledge is scattered across dozens of databases and vendor feeds joined by a fragile, near-capacity SSIS stack, with no trustworthy single customer record. This deliverable scopes the platform that fixes that — what it reads from, what it produces, how it is built, what it runs on, and what could go wrong — sitting above an already-decomposed build backlog.

### Source landscape and data model
- Three source tiers discovered in Phase 0 (SSIS review with Rick Sorich, 2026-06-08; database discovery, 2026-06-14): DAS internal SQL Server/RDS DBs, vendor APIs/feeds (21+ CRM providers, DMS aggregators, lead/review/enrichment feeds), and DAS app events — totaling ~85 distinct integrations (16 internal DBs + 69 new), each a tracked build story (`docs/source-onboarding-ledger.md`).
- Richest identity data is internal, e.g. Response Logix `oltp` (240 tables, 1.13B rows) with `franchise_consumer` (51M) and its alias graph (34M); legacy ETL spans 231 SQL objects across 20 modules (`docs/etl-data-inventory.md`).
- Output is one append-only, bitemporal golden record per person — Phase 1 deployment unit of 15 tables (11 core + 4 ML stubs), locked 2026-06-18 (Alicia + Luis); time-travel view was Mike Paylor's #1 requested artifact (`docs/cdp-architecture.md`).
- Scope stance: every source and channel is in scope for identity value (Dan Aston, 2026-06-17); field-level binding to concrete `db.schema.table.column` is a Phase 1 gate, not a Phase 0 blocker (27/34 fields mapped at discovery level).

### Integration and infrastructure
- SSIS (13 truncate-and-rebuild daily jobs) is being dropped — "not a reliable end source for the CDP" (Dan Aston, 2026-06-12); the CDP reimplements ingest against raw originals, never the EDW/DWRPT reporting views.
- Five reusable ingest primitives (DB-CDC, API, SFTP, webhook, CSV) over a config-driven registry feed one universal pipeline, so marginal cost per source keeps falling (Dan Aston, 2026-06-17).
- Target is a portable open-source core (Postgres, NATS JetStream, Temporal, OpenSearch, Airflow, Auth0) on Kubernetes; posture is dev baseline first, production rightsized on observed load (2026-06-16, `docs/cdp-reference-topology.md`).
- Cloud is a client choice: DAS prefers Azure (Dan Aston, 2026-06-17); the bake-off (`docs/cloud-aws-vs-azure-bakeoff.md`, costs re-verified 2026-06-22) finds the two clouds within ~3% — cost is not a blocker to Azure.

### Risk register
- Six risks each traced to `memory/decisions.md` / `memory/open-questions.md`: cross-cloud egress (~$90/mo, quantified at build), conflict-queue volume sized after 2-4 weeks of live measurement (Alicia + Luis, 2026-06-17), legacy `3BHS001` fragility (cautious read-replica extraction), unreliable all-zero CCID (deterministic Option A, locked 2026-06-17), and GLBA erasure via a tokenized PII vault — crypto-shred evaluated and rejected (Leo, 2026-06-21).
- Full document: `docs/deliverables/cdp-scoping-document.md`

components.title: Privacy-by-Design Framework for Dealer Data
components.summary: The framework that lets DAS pool consumer data across ~1,700 dealers while keeping each dealer's data invisible to every other dealer, honoring a deletion request, and proving compliance to a regulator — with isolation, centralized PII, and erasure satisfied by construction rather than bolted on. It matters because a CDP is where consumer data becomes most concentrated and most regulated, so a defensible deletion mechanism and airtight tenant isolation are existential to the platform, not optional polish.
components.detail:
DAS's CDP faces a built-in tension: it must resolve identity across dealers to be useful, yet keep each dealer's data invisible to every other dealer, and it must keep an append-only audit history while still being able to erase a person on request. This framework decides the *mechanisms* (isolation, where PII lives, how erasure works) and leaves *policy values* (retention periods, consent taxonomy, lawful-basis mapping) to Alicia + Luis with DAS Legal, who are not a Phase-0 blocker. It is deliberately deletion-first: the hard obligation is a defensible deletion, scoped against GLBA carve-outs.

### Regulatory frame and tenant isolation
- Frame is CCPA + TDPSA (Texas, effective 2024-07-01), the broader law: its deletion right covers data "obtained about" a consumer, not just first-party, which the source-granular provenance model covers by construction (`docs/deliverables/privacy-by-design-framework.md`).
- Deletion is **scoped, not unconditional** — GLBA-covered financial data (a material share, since dealers handle financing) is retained under an audited legal-basis hold; this is the single most important deviation from "delete everything."
- Isolation runs on PostgreSQL **Row-Level Security** (decided 2026-06-21, Leo), enforced on the tables so a forgotten `WHERE tenant_id =` cannot leak rows; shared-schema with a tenant discriminator, cost-effective at ~1,700 dealers. A negative test (no inference via field counts or response timing) is an acceptance criterion (`specs/02-phase-1-architecture/01-data-model/03-privacy-by-tenant.md`).

### PII vault and erasure
- All identity-class PII is centralized in one mutable **vault** keyed by surrogate token; everywhere else stores token + non-PII provenance only — so cross-store erasure becomes "delete the vault row" and every token dereferences to nothing.
- **No per-person keys**: crypto-shred / per-consumer DEKs were rejected as too complex, brittle, and expensive (decided 2026-06-21, Leo); erasure is a plain row delete. Provenance survives ("a phone was provided by the DMS on 2026-01-01" stays; only the number is gone — Leo's explicit requirement, 2026-06-21).
- Optional **salt + pepper** hardening, off by default, makes a backup/database-dump leak useless without the single external pepper (decided 2026-06-21, Leo). Tokenize at the CDP, not the edge (2026-06-21, Leo), concentrating protection where re-identification risk concentrates.
- Erasure runs as one durable **Temporal saga** (Option C2, approved 2026-06-19, Alicia) producing a single auditable completion record; backups age out by retention policy, not immediate scrub (2026-06-21, Leo).

### Consent, audit, and the policy-config layer
- Consent is first-class and **source-record granular**, so withdrawal on one channel removes exactly that source's records — per-channel, not whole-record (Dan Aston, 2026-06-17); typed + per-channel consent and the 30-day baseline retention window approved 2026-06-19 (Alicia); recorded in a tamper-evident SHA-256 hash-chained ledger (decided 2026-06-18, Leo) that holds pseudonymous references and survives erasure.
- A **policy-config layer** with deterministic resolution (raised 2026-06-21, Leo) sits over retention, salt+pepper toggle, suppression scope, edge-tokenization, and pepper scope (per-tenant by default, configurable to global) — DAS builds the layer, Legal populates the values.
- Full doc: `docs/deliverables/privacy-by-design-framework.md` (companion: `docs/deliverables/identity-resolution-strategy.md`; decision log: `memory/decisions.md`).

components.title: Identity Resolution Strategy & Identity Graph Plan
components.summary: The strategy for collapsing the same consumer's scattered records — a CRM lead, a DMS buyer, an email contact, a hashed ad-platform ID — into one auditable golden record per person, with the evidence for every link preserved. It matters because today DAS has no mechanism to recognize these fragments as one person ("we don't" resolve identity), so no one can answer what DAS actually knows about a given customer without manual stitching.
components.detail:
DAS identity resolution runs deterministic-first and earns intelligence later: Phase 1 ships exact matching on standardized identifiers plus a human review queue, and machine learning is deferred because DAS has no confirmed-match history to train on yet — the review decisions *become* that training data. The strategy is locked against a real-data bar set by Mike Paylor: *demonstrate* a golden record from DAS's actual data ("show me all the people that could be Mike"), not project model accuracy.

### Approach and resolution path
- Deterministic-first over an AI-first design, recorded as locked **Option A (2026-06-17, Luis + Alicia)**; leading with models would mean projecting accuracy on data that does not exist (`memory/decisions.md`).
- Every record runs standardize → match on strongest identifier → decide by confidence: high-confidence links automatically, ambiguous goes to the human review queue, no-match creates a new record. Orphan identifiers (e.g. a social ID with no email) are kept, not discarded, and resolve when a connecting record arrives.
- Bias is deliberately conservative — queue for review rather than risk a wrong merge, since wrong merges cost dealer trust far more than an extra record.

### The locked rules
- Survivorship ladder (**2026-06-18**): DMS is ground truth for transactions/name/address, CRM wins engagement and sales-relationship fields, enrichment ranks lowest; most-recent wins within a tier; no value is destroyed — losing values stay in history for audit and recompute (`specs/02-phase-1-architecture/01-data-model/05-survivorship-rules.md`).
- Households are detected, not assumed (hardest case per Dan): a shared canonical address plus a corroborating signal, human-confirmed before trusted.
- The legacy CommonClientID is not the foundation — a **2026-06-14 audit** found it non-functional (all-zero), so identity is built from first principles and the legacy ID is only a migration breadcrumb.

### What firms up on live data
- Locked: deterministic-first strategy, survivorship ladder, household model, and consent interaction; privacy/tenant isolation/erasure follow `docs/deliverables/privacy-by-design-framework.md`.
- Deferred to real traffic: exact confidence thresholds and review-queue volume — measured and tuned over the first weeks rather than guessed, shipping conservative defaults.
- Full deliverable: `docs/deliverables/identity-resolution-strategy.md`.

components.title: Detailed Phase 1 & Phase 2 Plans
components.summary: A stage-by-stage build plan that decomposes the CDP into sub-phases (1a platform slice, 1b long-tail migration, Phase 2 applications, Phase 3 AI/ML), each with relative T-shirt sizing and dependency-driven sequencing, plus an AWS-vs-Azure infrastructure run-cost model. It gives DAS a fixed-scope SOW foundation: what gets built in what order, how heavy each workstream is (~913 points / 456.5–894 engineering-days for Phase 1), and what the monthly cloud bill will be (~$1,140 dev / ~$4,460 prod).
components.detail:
Sequences the entire CDP build as overlapping sub-phases so value lands early rather than waiting on a full predecessor: 1a delivers a tested platform with one source per channel, 1b onboards the long tail, and Phase 2 deliberately starts at "critical data mass" before 1b finishes. All scope and sizing derive from the project backlog (`specs/manifest.json`), with the phase model and cost model as planning overlays on top.

### Phasing and sizing
- Six-stage model — 1a platform / 1b long-tail / Phase 2 enhancements / Phase 2 applicatives / 3a external AI / 3b own ML — sub-phased so downstream work overlaps instead of blocking (`specs/manifest.json` epics `phase-1-architecture`, `phase-1-build`, `phase-2-build`, `phase-3-ai-ml`).
- Phase 1a targets ~4 months, derived (scope effort ÷ modeled AI-assisted team capacity), not asserted — recomputes as scope/team firm up; the committed schedule is set in the SOW.
- Nine Phase 1 workstreams sized via relative T-shirt bands (S–EPIC) mapping to story-points and engineering-day ranges (`specs/estimate-bands.json`); totals computed live via `scripts/gen-estimates.py` into `specs/estimates.json`, never hand-entered — Phase 1 ≈ 913 points / 456.5–894 engineering-days. Heaviest: Foundation & Platform, Backend & Data Model, Ingest; the Long Tail carries the EPICs (SSIS reimplementation, report migration) and is sequenced last.

### Identity earned, not assumed
- Phase 1 ships deterministic matching plus a human-review queue; ML (3b: pairwise classifier, GNN/embeddings) is deferred until Phase 1's curation decisions produce training data — the locked "Option A, 2026-06-17" path (Luis + Alicia, per `docs/deliverables/identity-resolution-strategy.md`).
- AI/ML schema tables ship empty-but-complete in Phase 1, so 3a (reuse DAS's `ai.das-technology.com` layer) and 3b add with no migration.

### Infrastructure run-cost (AWS vs Azure)
- Build cost (effort) is separated from monthly run-cost; reference topology (rightsize-on-load, 2026-06-16): dev 3×4-vCPU + single-AZ Postgres, prod 6×8-vCPU + HA Postgres + read replica, self-hosted OSS core (NATS/Temporal/Airflow/OpenSearch/Jaeger).
- Baseline run-cost: dev ~$1,140 (AWS) / ~$1,150 (Azure); prod ~$4,460 / ~$4,590 — clouds ~3% apart at Postgres-native; managed warehouse roughly even since AWS's 4-RPU Redshift floor (Synapse pay-per-scan +$25–250 the cheapest query-driven lever; Redshift 4-RPU +$360–1,095 ≈ Azure Fabric). Unit rates first-party-verified 2026-06-22; quantities are estimates, so totals are ±30–40% planning figures, not a quote. Azure-primary preferred (DAS org cloud); no cloud decision recorded yet. Full pricing in `docs/cloud-aws-vs-azure-bakeoff.md`, sizing in `docs/cdp-reference-topology.md`.
- Full doc: `docs/deliverables/detailed-phase-1-2-plans.md`

deliverables.title: DAS Plan vs. CONFLICT Plan
deliverables.summary: A side-by-side of DAS's pre-discovery proposals (Architecture Plan v3, MVP spec v4) against the plan CONFLICT recommends after Phase 0 — what we kept, what we changed, and the finding or decision behind each change.
deliverables.detail:
DAS's v3/v4 were written against assumptions before the data, identity landscape, and infrastructure were examined; this plan is written against what Phase 0 surfaced. Every change is grounded in a finding or decision, not preference.

### What we kept
- Next.js frontend, PostgreSQL + RLS, the tiered resolution model, EAV+JSONB, and cloud-portability — the strong parts of v3 carry forward.

### What changed (highlights)
- **Identity** — AI-first to deterministic-first, ML earned in Phase 3 (no training data exists yet; Option A, 2026-06-17).
- **Ingestion** — a clean unified feed to original sources only, raw-first and replayable (DWRPT untrustworthy; SSIS deep-dive 2026-06-08).
- **Cloud** — Azure-only to a portable OSS core, Azure-primary preferred, bake-off decides (split estate).
- **Reporting** — Synapse/Juicebox to portable Postgres + Apache Superset (Juicebox not long-term; decided 2026-06-14).
- **Data model** — the 19-table v4 sketch to a 15-table day-1 set, zero migrations for Phase 2 (locked 2026-06-18).

### Source & evidence
- Full row-by-row delta: artifacts/phase-0/deliverables/das-cdp-revised-architecture-plan.md.
- DAS proposals: artifacts/phase-0/source-docs/. Decision log: memory/decisions.md.
